props.title: The Black Dahlia
props.initialSlug: 1940s noir thriller hunts LA's most brutal killer

sections.content: **The Black Dahlia** (2006) represents Brian De Palma's ambitious but flawed attempt to adapt James Ellroy's labyrinthine noir novel. Like De Palma's earlier **L.A. Confidential** (1997), it plunges into post-war Los Angeles's seedy underbelly, but with less cohesion. The film follows the real-life 1947 murder of Elizabeth Short, mirroring other noir-tinged true crime adaptations like **Zodiac** (2007) and **Chinatown** (1974). De Palma's signature visual flourishes - split diopter shots, elaborate tracking sequences - can't quite overcome the plot's overwhelming complexity.

sections.content: The film's greatest strength lies in its recreation of 1940s Hollywood, sharing DNA with **Hollywoodland** (2006) and **Devil in a Blue Dress** (1995). Vilmos Zsigmond's cinematography captures the era's shadowy menace, while production design by Dante Ferretti creates a believably corrupt Los Angeles. Josh Hartnett and Aaron Eckhart's detective duo follows noir tradition, though they lack the chemistry of similar pairings in **Seven** (1995) or **Kiss Kiss Bang Bang** (2005).

Where the film stumbles is in its handling of Elizabeth Short's story. Unlike more focused true crime adaptations like **Monster** (2003) or **Zodiac** (2007), De Palma gets lost in subplot tangents. Scarlett Johansson and Hilary Swank deliver committed performances, but their characters' arcs become muddled in the film's overwrought third act. The movie's treatment of violence against women occasionally feels exploitative, a criticism also leveled at De Palma's earlier works like **Dressed to Kill** (1980). sections.content: **The Black Dahlia** sits at an interesting intersection between classic noir and modern true crime drama. While films like **Memento** (2000) and **Brick** (2005) successfully reinvented noir conventions, De Palma sticks closer to traditional formulas. The result feels somewhat dated compared to more innovative genre entries like **Drive** (2011) or **Nightcrawler** (2014), which found fresh ways to explore Los Angeles's dark side.
